name: Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia / myeloid neoplasm with eosinophilia
aliases: chronic eosinophilic leukaemia not otherwise specified
myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusion

reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterised by persistent peripheral eosinophilia with evidence of clonality or increased blasts
End-organ damage from eosinophil degranulation, particularly cardiac (endomyocardial fibrosis), pulmonary, cutaneous and neurological, drives morbidity
A key step is identifying rearrangements of PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1 or PCM1-JAK2, which define a distinct treatable category
The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, arising from a cryptic deletion on chromosome 4, is exquisitely sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibition
Diagnosis requires exclusion of reactive causes such as parasitic infection, allergy, drug reaction and other malignancies
A raised serum tryptase and marrow features may accompany PDGFRA-rearranged disease and can mimic mastocytosis
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion once clonal and reactive causes are ruled out
reference.pathophysiology: This group of disorders results from clonal proliferation of eosinophil precursors, most often driven by constitutively active tyrosine kinases created by gene rearrangements involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1 or JAK2. These fusion kinases signal continuously to expand the eosinophil lineage independent of normal cytokine control. Where no specific rearrangement is found but clonality or increased blasts are demonstrable, the disorder is classified as chronic eosinophilic leukaemia not otherwise specified. Sustained eosinophilia releases granule proteins that injure tissues, with the heart being especially vulnerable to progressive endomyocardial fibrosis and thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Lymphocyte-variant hypereosinophilia driven by an aberrant T-cell clone
Other myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic neoplasms with eosinophilia
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film to confirm and quantify eosinophilia
Molecular and cytogenetic testing for PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1 and PCM1-JAK2 abnormalities
Serum tryptase and marrow examination for clonality and blast count
Echocardiography and cardiac troponin to assess eosinophilic heart disease
T-cell receptor studies and lymphocyte immunophenotyping for the lymphocytic variant
Screening for reactive causes including parasitic serology
redFlags: Cardiac symptoms or troponin rise indicating eosinophilic myocardial damage
Thromboembolic events from the hypereosinophilic state
Rising blast count suggesting progression to acute leukaemia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the molecular subtype; PDGFRA- and PDGFRB-rearranged disease responds dramatically to tyrosine kinase inhibition with excellent outcomes, whereas FGFR1-rearranged and blast-phase disease is aggressive with poorer survival.
pitfalls: Labelling clonal eosinophilia as idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome without molecular testing
Missing the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, which is highly treatable but cytogenetically cryptic
Overlooking early cardiac involvement before symptoms develop
Attributing persistent eosinophilia solely to allergy or parasites
